en: Non-violence, non-stealing, and likewise celibacy—this is the threefold virtuous action pertaining to the body. Avoiding untruthful, malicious, and harsh speech—this fourfold restraint pertains to speech. (Jātakamālāṭīkā 17.1.5)
When this restraint, which has the abstinence from intoxicants as its eighth [member], is endowed with a pure livelihood, then one is established in the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*);
otherwise, the wise declare it to be immorality (*dauḥśīlya*).

Through deficient morality one goes to a miserable rebirth; in the human world, through mild [morality] one is born [as a human]; but through middling [morality] one proceeds to the sixfold state of the celestial dwellers whose minds are liberated from desire. Likewise, established in superior morality and settled in the fourfold method of meditative concentration, [one attains higher realms].
Therefore, he abides with superior intensity in that fourfold method of attaining the virtuous meditative absorptions.
When, however, he maintains pure morality— untouched, unbroken, unblemished, and praised by the virtuous—
then he gradually attains the feverless Nirvana, which is auspicious, peaceful, unshakable, and imperishable.
Just as the earth is the foundation for all embodied beings—whether trees or even creeping plants—so too is conduct said to be the supreme foundation for all auspicious deeds upon this earth.
(17.1.10) *cf. Buddhacarita 23.17*
For just as a lame man might have the impulse to walk, or one whose wings are lost might have the power to soar in the sky,
or just as there might be a desire to cross over without a boat, so too would a fortunate rebirth come to pass without virtuous conduct. (17.1.11)

Let him subsist on roots and fruits, or let him find contentment with grass-blades like the deer; let him feed on milk alone, or even on water and air— if his character is ruined, he is not purified by these means.

Let them wear the tonsure or indeed let them carry only tufts of hair; let them bear matted locks drenched with the water of ritual bathing; or let them wander clad in garments of many varied forms—if they are devoid of virtuous conduct, this is merely a mockery. (17.1.13) % cf. Buddhacarita 23.21
In the cold season, let him enter the water, or let him ascend a blazing fire;
or let him cast his body from the heights of a mountain—if he lacks moral discipline, death alone is his only [reward]. (17.1.14)
Let him go away to the Gaṅgā, or approach the lakes, let him go to the Sarasvatī or to the Puṣkara ponds; [in the text:
*paraitu*].

Whether one frequents Naimiṣa or Gayā, if one’s conduct is ruined, the labor is fruitless. Or let him plunge into the water three times [daily], or offer oblations into the fire according to the rules at the three junctions of the day.
Let him experience exhaustion in the practice of recitation, vows, sacrifices, and the like, or let him not; it matters nothing if he is impaired by his moral conduct.
Let him go to old age upon the backs of celestial chariots, or let him roam about adorned in white garments.

Let him eat whatever specific food he desires; and established in virtue, he shall abide in the three heavens. Whether one is born of the twice-born caste or born of a low womb, if he observes virtuous conduct, he goes to the triple heaven.
Whether one is born of the twice-born caste or born of a low womb, if he abandons moral conduct, he does not attain perfection.
For even a Śūdra who possesses good conduct goes to heaven, while a twice-born man who has fallen from his conduct does not go there.
Indeed, by means of firm moral conduct, the sage Mataṅga, though born of a base womb, shines in the third heaven.
Just as a lake filled with water but containing serpents, or a tree with blossoming branches yet covered in thorns,
so too is a man who, though endowed with learning, beauty, and noble birth, is averse to virtuous conduct.
For those born of noble lineage, folly here is death; for those superior in sacred learning, pride is death.

But for men whose character is entirely ruined, there is a terrible death both in this world and in the next. Indeed, it is better to be poor but possessed of virtue than to be wealthy yet unadorned with good qualities.

For even in a state of poverty, the flavor of virtues praised by the virtuous excels nectar. (17.1.22) Indeed, the fragrance of a virtuous person praised does not scatter like that of a flower garland, nor does its scent waft like that of an ointment.
Just as the unsurpassed fragrance consisting of the moral conduct of the virtuous wafts unceasingly both in heaven and here on earth;
[so too] in this world there is self-satisfaction, a favorable rebirth from others, renown, popularity, and indeed great honor.
The great seers know that such happiness is indeed the manifold fruit of ethical discipline pertaining to the present life.
For one who possesses virtue and desires excellence, or even birthlessness, or auspiciousness, these are not far off.
For the mental aspiration of a man of pure conduct, whose self is directed toward that [goal], comes to fulfillment.
Likewise, seeing the immoral man suffering, ruined by execution, imprisonment, calamities, and the like—
Thinking, "This person will not find fault with me for now," the virtuous man attains satisfaction for this reason as well.

(17.1.26) When men who love virtue praise those possessed of virtue, saying, "Oh, how worthy of homage they are! the virtuous man experiences great joy, thinking, "I too possess such auspicious qualities. (17.1.27)
When the time of destruction has arrived, amidst intense agonies and weeping kinsmen,
the virtuous man who is at peace, thinking "these pure virtues are mine," encounters no fear of death.
For virtue is the supreme medicine for diseases, protection in times of fear, and a kinsman in times of calamity.
A lamp in the darkness, a bridge over difficult terrain, and a raft in the great, bottomless waters of death—
thus has morality been extolled here by me, according to my ability, having examined the treatise in accordance with reality.
And for the purpose of exhorting men of bad character, and for the sake of establishing the stability of those of good character. (17.1.30)
